title: Volume of Spheres

blocks.html: A sphere has no flat base to stack, so the cylinder trick needs a twist. More than 2,000 years ago, Archimedes compared a sphere with a cylinder and a cone that just fit around it.

A sphere of radius $r$ fits snugly in a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $2r$. That cylinder holds $\pi r^{2} \cdot 2r = 2\pi r^{3}$, and a cone with the same base and height holds one third as much, $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}$. Archimedes showed that the cone and the sphere together hold exactly as much as the cylinder. So the sphere holds $2\pi r^{3} - \frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$: the cone, sphere and cylinder are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$.

blocks.name: g8-solid
blocks.cap: A cone, a sphere and a cylinder with the same radius and height $2r$. Change $r$; the ratio stays $1 : 2 : 3$.

blocks.html: $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$ Cube the radius (not the diameter), then multiply by $\frac{4}{3}\pi$.

blocks.q: Find the volume of a sphere with radius 3 cm.

blocks.q: A ball has diameter 12 inches. Find its volume.

blocks.title: Half a sphere
blocks.q: A bowl is a hemisphere with radius 6 cm. How much can it hold?

blocks.title: Work backward
blocks.q: A sphere has volume $36\pi$. Find its radius.
steps: $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = 36\pi$. Divide by $\pi$ and multiply by $\frac{3}{4}$: $r^{3} = 27$.

blocks.html: Squaring the radius instead of cubing it, or cubing the diameter. Volume is three-dimensional, so the radius appears three times. With the diameter 12, cubing 12 instead of 6 makes the answer 8 times too big.
